utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good morning, everybody. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-83-T, the Prosecutor versus Rasim Delic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have the appearances, please, starting with the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. Daryl Mundis and Kyle Wood for the Prosecution, assisted by our case manager, Alma Imamovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. VIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning to my learned friends from the Office of the Prosecutor. Vasvija Vidovic and Nicholas Robson, representing General Rasim Delic, with our legal assistant, Lana Deljkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Good morning, sir. May the witness please make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. You may be seated, sir. Make sure you're comfortable, and good morning to you. Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. Alispahic is appearing for purposes of cross-examination under Rule 92 bis, so the Prosecution has no questions, his statement having been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And even before we do that, may I just put on the record that we continue to sit pursuant to Rule 15 bis, as Judge Harhoff is not available today. Thank you very much. Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Alispahic. My name is Nicholas Robson. I represent General Delic, and I'll be asking you some questions today. Just by way of explanation: During the course of this case, you gave three statements to investigators from the Office of the Prosecution. Two of those statements, dated the 22nd of December, 2005, and the 27th of January, 2006, have already been admitted into evidence before this Trial Chamber. Those are your second and third statements. The first statement that you gave to the Office of the Prosecution was dated the 7th of November, 2004. That statement has not been admitted. There are some details within that statement that I will be asking you about today. Just starting with some background questions, if I may. It's right that during the war, you joined the Territorial Defence in May 1992, and soon after that time you went to an army training centre in Zenica, where you were there until February 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And after February 1993, you joined the 3rd Military Police Battalion of the 3rd Corps of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your statements, you explained that the 3rd Military Police Battalion was composed of different units. There were two companies, a traffic company, a logistics platoon, and a services platoon. You were a member of the Services Platoon; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And the Services Platoon was responsible for on-site criminal investigations?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And it's right that the commander of the 3rd Military Police Battalion was Zaim Mujezinovic?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, below Commander Mujezinovic, but above you in the hierarchy of the Military Police Battalion, was the commander of the Services Platoon; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Before you joined the 3rd Military Police Battalion, am I right in saying that at no stage had you received any relevant training or experience to enable you to carry out your duties properly within the Services Platoon?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And is it correct that most of your colleagues in the Services Platoon also lacked training and skills to enable them to carry out their role properly?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: 60 per cent weren't.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Concerning your role in the Services Platoon, am I right in saying that you had a duty to investigate when it appeared that a crime had been committed by a member of the ARBiH?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in addition to carrying out criminal investigation, is it right that the Services Platoon could occasionally be ordered to collect prisoners of war and transport them to the Reception Centre at Zenica KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In relation to the 3rd Military Police Battalion, am I correct in saying that there were two lines of command, so within the command-and-control line, command was carried out by the corps commander; however, within the professional line, it was carried out by the assistant commander for security of the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Concerning the collection of prisoners of war and transportation to the Reception Centre, is it right that instructions would normally be received through the professional line of reporting?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Concerning the collection and transportation of prisoners of war, am I right in saying that you would normally receive instructions through the professional line of reporting; in other words, instructions would normally originate with the assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I received orders from my immediate supervisor. I don't know where he had gotten them from. I wouldn't be able to tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. In your statements, you refer to two occasions when you collected prisoners of war from the El Mujahedin Detachment. You refer to one occasion when you took over some women of Serb ethnicity from the El Mujahedin Detachment at the Vatrostalna facility. You also talk about another occasion when you collected a number of captured Serb soldiers from the El Mujahedin Detachment camp in Zavidovici Municipality. Do you recall explaining about those two occasions?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I remember when I provided my statement to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in your statement, you said that those were the only occasions that you had dealings with the El Mujahedin Detachment in relation to prisoners of war; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. I want to turn, first of all, to the occasion when you collected the three women. In your second statement given to the Office of the Prosecution, you explain how you went to the El Mujahedin Detachment facility at Vatrostalna. Is it right that there was you and a driver that went to collect the women?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In that statement, you say the following. This is after you've collected the women: "Once we..." --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you give us the date and paragraph that you are reading from, sir; The date of the statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's the second statement, which is the 22nd of December, 2005, and it's paragraph 38.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, in the statement, you say: "Once we moved away from the Mujahedin camp, I told the ladies to remove the blindfolds and asked them whether they were maltreated in any way. They replied in the negative." Now I want to ask you some questions about that. Having collected these three women, am I right in saying that, before they were taken to the Reception Centre for Prisoners of War, you, first of all, took them into the Service Platoon office?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So the Service Platoon office is where your unit was based. Is that office located close to or actually inside KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Which is it; is it actually within the KP Dom compound?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Our unit was billeted in one part of the KP Dom. We were separated from the civilian part.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So you had the opportunity to speak to the three women during the journey and also at the Service Platoon office. Do you remember asking them if they had been mistreated?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. As we went to the main road, when I told them to remove their blindfolds, Resa [as interpreted] was a member of the army or brought from some unit, and when we brought those two -- three women, the practice was to ask them whether they had been ill-treated, hurt, whether they had any objections. I asked them, and I received a negative answer. There were no traces on them of any physical abuse, and they indeed confirmed that they hadn't been ill-treated, at least at that moment. That's what they said to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You just mentioned a name there. The record didn't capture the name. Could you repeat for us who was the member of the army that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: I did not mention any names. I said that even when we brought in army members to our unit on such grounds, we were duty-bound to ask them whether they had been ill-treated or hurt. I'm talking within that context. I'm telling you that our every encounter with persons that we brought in meant that they would be asked whether they were ill-treated or hurt, and I never mentioned any names. I said that "whoever," whichever member of the army was brought in. I can illustrate this by saying that, if somebody was in an army unit and we were supposed to bring that person into our centre, it was our duty to ask them whether they had been hurt in the place where they had been staying before having been brought to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you for that clarification. You just said that, "Even when we brought in army members to our unit on such grounds, we were duty-bound to ask them whether they had been ill-treated or hurt." Can you just explain which army members you're talking about; members of which army?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: The regular army, members of the BiH Army unit. For example, if they had deserted or something else, we would bring them into our centre. It was our common practice to ask them that within that context.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And just for clarification, that would also apply to prisoners of war from --

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. On two occasions, when I brought them in, I had to ask them because certain forms had to be filled in to show whether they had any traces of ill-treatment on their bodies, whether on reception they had shown traces of previous ill-treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. We're going to look at some of the documentation that you completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this stage, perhaps we could go into private session, as we remain on the topic of the three ladies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the Chamber please move into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'd now like to turn to the subject of the prisoners of war, the men that you collected.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we just get confirmation that we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, now we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Yes. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, according to paragraph 22 of your first statement, dated the 17th of November, 1994 [sic], you said the following about the Serb prisoners of war: "I went to the second..." -- Sorry, I apologise. 17th of November of 2004 is the date of the statement. That's my mistake.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. I was just saying is he dealing with paragraph 22.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in that paragraph, you state: "I went to the second gate, where the 12 VRS soldiers were lined up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Are you starting from the middle of the paragraph or where? Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You have it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: You state: "I went to the second gate, where the 12 VRS soldiers were lined up. I took them over and brought them with the minibus to my office at the Service Platoon. I wrote down their names; and, after that, they were handed over to the Gathering Centre of Prisoners of War." Is that correct, what you told the investigator in that statement?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It's unclear to me, totally, the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps we could bring up the statement on the screen and show the witness. That might be the easiest. So the statement is D732. It's page 4 in English and page 4 in the B/C/S version. Perhaps before I ask Mr. Alispahic to look at paragraph 22, perhaps we can look at the first page to confirm that it is, indeed, his statement made in November 2004. Could we just go to the first page in both documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So would you agree with me, Mr. Alispahic, that what we can see here is what appears to be a statement given by you on the 17th of November, 2004?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we can scroll to the bottom of the English version, where I hope we can see there's a signature.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And that's your signature we can see there under --

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can go back to page 4 in both versions, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in is the part of the statement, and it's towards the end of paragraph 22. I hope it's on your page. Do you see the part that says: "I went to the second gate, where 12 VRS soldiers were lined up. I took them over and brought them with the minibus to my office at the Services Platoon. I wrote down their names; and, after that, they were handed over to the Gathering Centre of Prisoners of War." Do you see that part of the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you agree that what you said there is correct; in other words, you collected the prisoners of war, you took them to your office at the Services Platoon, and there you wrote down their names and took information from them?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, as with the three Serb women, once again you had the opportunity to speak to these prisoners during the course of the journey, and, also, you had the chance to see them and speak with them while you were at the Service Platoon office; am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, then, if we can look at this final sentence in paragraph 22, what it states is: "I could not see any injuries or bruises on these 12 VRS soldiers. I also asked them if they had been maltreated, but they denied." Do you see that part of your statement?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And do you stand by what you told the investigator when you gave the statement?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: In a brief conversation with them, that's what it says, and it's correct what is written down, meaning that they told me that they had not been mistreated or hurt.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I could show the witness a document at this stage, it's P2682.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess that you're not tendering D732. It's a statement, anyway.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Correct, Your Honour, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, could you confirm that this is a document from the 3rd Military Police Battalion, dated the 29th of September, 1995, and the subject is: "Taking over members of the so-called VRS from the El Mujahedin Detachment"?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could look at page 2 in the B/C/S version and page 3 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Can you confirm that that is your signature on this document?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can return back to the first page of both documents, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: As we saw a little earlier with the three Serb women, am I right in saying that, once again, this is an Official Note listing the names of the persons that you brought into the Reception Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And in the English version, if we could just look at page 2, just to confirm the names. If we could scroll down the page in this document, please, and if we could look at the final page in English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So what we can see here is the name of the three Serb men that were brought in; is that so -- Sorry, I beg your pardon, the ten Serb men that were brought in?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, when we looked -- when we discussed the three Serb women a little earlier, we saw that, for each person, you filled out a form which described whether there were any signs of sickness or injury. Would a similar form have been completed in respect of each of these ten Serb prisoners of war?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, if you had seen any injuries or signs of mistreatment on those soldiers, that would have been entered and recorded onto that sheet; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes, because they would not have been admitted to the centre if there were any injuries on them that we did not report or note down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, if this document could please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: P2682 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 948.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we could now turn to Exhibit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry. Just before we remove the document from the screen, did I hear you say, Mr. Robson, that the people on that list were ten?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, according to this document that we just saw a moment ago, there were ten names mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can I just double-check something with the witness. Witness, in your statement that Mr. Robson has been discussing with you, at paragraph 22, you talk of "12 VRS soldiers." Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible that in the first statement, it was said "12," but this is the correct information that was written down of those who were brought in. It means that on the basis of a report on taking over persons, it was said that there were such-and-such a number of them, but exactly the number of persons that I took over was ten.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Let's try and reconcile your statements, then, or at least get an explanation. Do I understand you to say that this ten is the same number that you are referring to in your statement dated the 27th of January, 2006, at paragraph 4, where you say: "I remember that I went to the Mujahedin camp when I took over ten to 11 Serb prisoners of war"? Are you talking about the same incident here in this paragraph and in the other paragraph in the other statement, paragraph 22?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I gave my statement, I didn't remember, I didn't know the number of persons involved when this was presented.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I understand, Mr. Alispahic, and I'm not trying to tie you down to numbers. I just want to know that what you refer to in paragraph 4 of your statement of 2006 is the same incident that you are referring to in your statement of 2004. Are you talking about the same incident? The reason I'm asking you is --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Thank you so much. You may proceed, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. If we could look at Exhibit 875, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Alispahic, a moment ago, we looked at an Official Note relating to the hand-over of the ten prisoners of war. Can you confirm that what we see before us now is a transfer list relating to the same ten persons, and it's dated the 29th of September, 1995?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And, again, is this yet another form that you had to complete when the men were brought into the Reception Centre?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is the document used to be handed over to the admittance centre, because otherwise they would not be able to be -- or they could not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So from these documents, what we can conclude is that at every stage from the moment you took the prisoners of war, there was a record to show what happened to the prisoners; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at this list of prisoners, we can see two names there: Milorad Panjic [sic] and Nedja [sic] Pecanac.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I will come to these two names in a moment, if I may. Your Honours, if that document could be put away, I'd like to turn to P2687, P2687. This is the correct document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Alispahic, the B/C/S version of this document is a little hard to see, but -- and I can supply you with a hard copy, if necessary. But would you agree with me that what this document is a report from the 3rd Corps Security Services to the General Staff Security Administration?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Based on what is written here, it should be the way you suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And we can see a heading that says: "Results of the preliminary interview with Prisoners of War Milorad Panic and Nedja [sic] Pecanac."

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we could just look at page 2 in the B/C/S version and page 2 in the English as well -- I beg your pardon. If we could go back to page 1 in the B/C/S version, and if we can scroll down the page in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this document bears the signature block of Agan Haseljic, who is the assistant commander for security in the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So this document relates to a preliminary interview with those two men that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: If we can now look at page 3 in the English and page 2 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that this is a second document that is appended to that first document from the assistant commander for security?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This is probably just one component. It was based on this conversation that the document was produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, let's have a look at the second document accompanying Commander Haseljic's report. Would you agree with me that this document --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just so that we can follow, where is it being deduced from these documents that there is a second document? We are left behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, what I'll do is I'll first just establish what this second document is, and then I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But when you say to him, "When you look at this document, can you see that there is a second document," what must he look at in this document to see that there is a second document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'll clarify that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, a moment ago, we saw a report from the 3rd Corps Military Security Service. Would you agree with me that when we look at this document, this is a separate -- this is a second document, or certainly appears to be, dated the 30th of September, 1995, and it has a heading: "Conduct of the preliminary interview with the members of the so-called 'VRS'- Milorad Panic and Nedja [sic] Pecanac"?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It's a male, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I'm told that the name is "Nedjo Pecanac."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: On the previous document, was it not Milorad "Pajic," not "Panic"?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Milorad is the first name, I believe, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But was this surname not spelled with a "J" instead of an "N," in the previous document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I believe it was, but if I can just try and ascertain what this document is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, you agree that we have a document in front of you that has a subject heading: "Conduct of preliminary interview with ..." two named persons? Would you like to see a hard copy of this, if it's hard to make it out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I do think it's very hard to make out, this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could please turn to the second page, the next page in this document that we have on our screens in the B/C/S version, and the last page in the English, page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, Mr. Alispahic, this second document that we have just looked at, would you agree that you are the author of that document?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So if we can go back to the page before in the B/C/S version and page 3 in the English version. Page 3 in the English, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So as you are the author of this document, which relates to a --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is this page 3 of the English?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour, it's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So as you are the author of this document, which relates to a preliminary interview with the two named persons, is it correct to say that you carried out an interview with them?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if we look at the first paragraph of this document, we can see that you carried out that interview on the 30th of September, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And if you could please take a look through the contents of this document, and if you could take the opportunity to read both pages of the B/C/S version. Could you please confirm, if you're able to do so, that nowhere in this document does it suggest that these two Serb prisoners of war were mistreated in any way?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we turn over the English page so that we can keep reading.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Have you had the chance to read the document?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It's a poor copy. Well, I managed to some extent, but not everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Again, if you'd like a hard copy, Mr. Alispahic, I can supply you with one.

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, perhaps would you like to see the third page in English, just to read the contents of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can we scroll down the English, please, or turn it around. Go to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So can you confirm, Mr. Alispahic, that nowhere in your document does it suggest that these two men were mistreated at any stage during their detention?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: And then just to round off this document - if we could return back to the first page in the English and B/C/S version - we saw that your interview was carried out on the 30th of September; and, in this first document entitled "Report," this is also dated the 30th of September, the heading being: "Results of the preliminary interview with prison Prisoners of War Milorad Panic and Nedjo Pecanac," would you agree that this report to the General Staff Security Administration seems to be based on your preliminary interview? Are you able to say?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: It probably is.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, could this document please be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, Exhibit number 949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Your Honour, I note the time. Perhaps it would be a good moment to take the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. We'll take the break and come back at quarter to 11.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Mr. Alispahic, in your statements, you discuss the El Mujahedin Detachment. Would you agree with me that the El Mujahedin Detachment did not have its own military police unit?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your first statement of the 17th of November, 2004, at paragraph 17, you say that: "I have never investigated a crime committed by a soldier from an Arabic country." Am I correct in stating that, during the time you served in the 3rd Military Police Battalion, you had no reason to investigate any member of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your second statement, which was taken in 2005, you talk about the security organ of the El Mujahedin Detachment. Now, initially, in paragraph 31, you state: "The security organ of the El Mujahedin was a foreigner." When we read that statement, we can see that at that point, when you were interviewed, you could not recall the name of that person who was the security organ. As we read through the statement, at paragraph 44, it becomes clear that the investigator showed you a photograph of a man; and on that photograph, the name "Abu Aiman" was written. You then recognised that man as being the security organ of the El Mujahedin Detachment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's how he introduced himself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So did you ever see anything official, such as a document or anything in writing, that showed that Abu Ajman was the security organ of the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Was it Abu Ajman himself who told you that he was the security organ of the detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Well, we talked, and he probably said that. We talked on the phone, and he said that he was working with the security. Was he ever appointed or not is something that I can't tell you. That's what he said. I'm not sure if it's true or not, but that's what he said. I never saw this written anywhere in a document or anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have any personal knowledge of whether Abu Ajman sent reports to the Military Security Service of the 3rd Corps or any other unit?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that the El Mujahedin Detachment did not have a security service or security organ like other ARBiH units?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Believe me, I don't know how they were organised. I never saw a chart or anything like that, and I don't know how it functioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: In your second statement from 2005, at paragraph 76 of the statement, you state: "I might have had approximately 50 meetings with Aiman." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: How many meetings did you, in fact, have with Abu Ajman? Can you remember?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: This figure here was stated in the last statement I made, which I signed. As I was signing, I told them that the figure was erroneous. The Prosecutor, who was talking to me -- or rather, the interpreter explained to me that this wasn't material. I think there was a total of between five and ten meetings, in my estimate, in the barracks with the Military Police Battalion and the two times I went to see them over there. Ajman and I never met anywhere else, aside from the barracks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So, if you only had between five and ten meetings with Abu Ajman, and that included the two occasions when you took over the Serb prisoners of war, would I be correct in saying that you had only limited involvement with the El Mujahedin Detachment?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Yes. I only had involvement with the detachment when I received orders from my superior.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: So would you agree that, from your limited involvement with the El Mujahedin Detachment, this particular detachment did not, in fact, appear to be a regular unit of the 3rd Corps, like other ARBiH units that you had to deal with?

utterances.speaker: ZAKIR ALISPAHIC
utterances.text: Based on my work, based on what I saw, they didn't have the same structure. They weren't organised the same way as us; and by "us," I mean the regular units. Whenever we went there, they gave us whatever information they thought was necessary and any explanations that they cared to give us as to why they were doing certain things. But as far as I know, they weren't structured the same way as all the other units. I'm not really familiar with their structure; but during our brief meetings, that was my impression.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBSON
utterances.text: I have no further questions for him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Wood.

utterances.speaker: MR. WOOD
utterances.text: Nothing, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Wood. Judge. Sir, thank you very much. This brings us to the conclusion of your testimony. Thank you very much for coming to testify. You are now released. You may go, you may stand down, you are excused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, as we previously had informed the Trial Chamber's legal officer, we have no further witnesses for today. The next witness who's scheduled to appear tomorrow is travelling today, so we have nothing further for today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. In that event, then, the Court will stand adjourned until tomorrow at 9.00 in the morning in Courtroom II. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 5th day of December, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 23 24

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 10.55 a.m.,
